hook.text: One finch species reached the Galápagos. Millions of years later, 13 species with wildly different beaks exist.

buildup.text: Adaptive radiation occurs when one lineage rapidly diversifies to fill many ecological niches.

discovery.text: Hawaiian honeycreepers evolved from a single ancestor into nectar-feeders, seed-crackers, and insect-probers.

twist.text: Cichlid fish in African lakes evolved over 500 species in under 2 million years—one of the fastest radiations known.

climax.text: Empty niches after extinctions or island colonization trigger the most dramatic radiations.

punchline.text: One ancestor, many descendants. Opportunity drives diversity.

details.summary: Adaptive radiation occurs when a single ancestral species rapidly diversifies into many forms to fill available ecological niches. Darwin's finches on the Galapagos Islands are the classic example, evolving different beak shapes to exploit seeds, insects, and cacti.
details.whyItMatters: Adaptive radiation explains how biodiversity arises after mass extinctions or when organisms colonize new environments. It demonstrates that ecological opportunity, not just mutation, drives the pace and direction of evolutionary change.
takeaways: Darwin's finches evolved 18 species from one ancestor on the Galapagos
Radiation accelerates when empty niches become available after extinctions
Key innovations like flight or flowers can trigger major adaptive radiations

faq.question: What triggers adaptive radiation?
faq.answer: Empty ecological niches are the main trigger, created by mass extinctions, colonization of new islands, or key innovations that open new ways of life. After dinosaurs vanished, mammals rapidly diversified to fill vacated niches across land, sea, and air.

faq.question: How fast does adaptive radiation happen in evolutionary terms?
faq.answer: Remarkably fast. Cichlid fish in East African lakes produced hundreds of species in just tens of thousands of years. Hawaiian honeycreepers diversified from one colonist into over 50 species. Geological isolation and open niches accelerate the process enormously.
